source: Zhou et al. (2024) Interpretable Differential Diagnosis with Dual-Inference LLMs (Dual-Inf)
finding: Prompt framework with a forward module (symptoms to diagnoses) and a backward module (diagnosis back to expected symptoms), plus examination and self-reflection. It beat chain-of-thought baselines on a new 570-note differential diagnosis set.
numbers: Open-XDDx: 570 notes, 9 specialties, mean 4.6 diagnoses per note. GPT-4 diagnostic accuracy Dual-Inf 0.533 vs SC-CoT 0.472 (diff 0.061, 95% CI 0.055-0.062). Interpretation accuracy 0.446 vs 0.334 (SC-CoT). GPT-4o interpretation 0.488 vs 0.408. Averaged over 5 runs.
quote: enable LLMs to conduct bidirectional inference (i.e., from symptoms to diagnoses and vice versa)
limits: Text-only exam-style notes, not real EHR. Baselines (CoT, Diagnosis-CoT, SC-CoT, Self-Contrast) differ in more than direction. Automatic grading by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Cheap template: after proposing hypotheses, recall each hypothesis's expected findings and check them against the case.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Dual-Inf ablation of the backward module
finding: Ablation: forward-only and variants without reflection scored lower. Full Dual-Inf added about 7 points over the variant without the backward module (FI-EM).
numbers: GPT-4 diagnostic accuracy: FI, FI-EM* and Dual-Inf* all below 0.46; FI-EM approached 0.5; full Dual-Inf about 7% higher than FI-EM. Interpretation: BERTScore +24%, METEOR +28% over Dual-Inf* (no reflection).
limits: Backward module and reflection loop are confounded in some variants. Table 3 cells were not cleanly parsed from the PDF text; the 7% is the paper's own summary.
agent_relevance: Backward check helps most when paired with a loop that feeds low-confidence hypotheses back to the forward step.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Dual-Inf on rare diseases and error types
finding: Gain from bidirectional inference holds on rare diseases and cuts missing-content errors, but the reported factual-error count went up.
numbers: Rare-disease subset, GPT-4: DDx accuracy CoT 0.396, SC-CoT 0.425, Dual-Inf 0.483. GPT-4o: 0.491 vs 0.431 (SC-CoT). Error analysis on 100 cases: missing content 89+ (SC-CoT) vs about 76 (Dual-Inf); factual errors 8.2 (SC-CoT) vs 17 (Dual-Inf); low relevance 10.8 vs 15.4.
limits: The text as read gives Dual-Inf MORE factual and low-relevance errors than SC-CoT in this 100-case count, while the paper's summary says it made fewer. The mismatch is unresolved.
agent_relevance: Backward recall can add content but also wrong content; needs a verifier.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Dual-Inf human evaluation
finding: Clinicians rated Dual-Inf explanations higher on correctness, completeness and usefulness (1-5 scale, 100 notes, GPT-4).
numbers: Completeness: Dual-Inf 38 scores of 3 and 21 of 4 vs SC-CoT 19 and 3. Usefulness: 33 of 3 and 25 of 4 vs 26 and 10. Correctness mostly 3-4 vs 2-3.
limits: Small human sample; blinding not stated in the text read; raw counts.
agent_relevance: Supports adding a backward expected-findings step for explanation quality, not just accuracy.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Dual-Inf iterative self-reflection loop
finding: Low-confidence diagnoses from the examination module go back to the forward module. Most notes were revised iteratively, and accuracy rose across iterations on ten sampled five-iteration notes.
numbers: Median per-note accuracy Dual-Inf 0.495 (75th percentile 0.746) vs SC-CoT 0.434 (0.652) and Diagnosis-CoT 0.421 (0.628), GPT-4.
limits: Iteration trace shown only for ten notes; no cost or latency reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Loop shape: forward, backward recall, examine, feed back weak hypotheses.

source: Zeng et al. (2024) MSDiagnosis: multi-step clinical diagnosis benchmark with forward/backward framework
finding: Benchmark of Chinese admission records with five questions (primary diagnosis, basis, differential, final diagnosis, basis). Framework runs forward inference with similar-case examples, then backward inference, reflection and refinement.
numbers: 2,225 cases, 12 departments. Removing backward inference cut final-diagnosis F1 by 2.28 points and macro-recall by 2.27 points (Table 5 ablation). Final F1 34.32 full vs 32.04 without backward inference.
quote: backward reasoning effectively enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of the final diagnosis
limits: Authors' own framework on own benchmark; Chinese records; absolute F1 is low (about 34); gain is small.
agent_relevance: A small but real gain; backward verification is not a large lever on hard real records.

source: Zeng et al. (2024) MSDiagnosis: ablation of primary and differential steps
finding: Final diagnosis quality depends on the early step. Errors in the first (forward) answer propagate. Multi-step helps interpretability more than accuracy.
numbers: Final F1 where primary matches final: multi-step 39.33 (w/o primary 44.46, w/o differential 41.28). Where primary differs from final: multi-step 18.12 vs 21.17 (w/o primary) and 18.78 (w/o differential). Differential-diagnosis F1 only about 8-11.
limits: In several cells removing intermediate steps scored HIGHER than the full multi-step run.
agent_relevance: Anchoring on the first hypothesis hurts; sequencing steps does not by itself fix it.

source: MedEinst (2026) Benchmarking the Einstellung effect in medical LLMs
finding: Counterfactual pairs built from DDXPlus: a control case and a trap case that differ only in discriminating evidence. Strong LLMs fall into the stereotypical diagnosis in the trap case. This is a machine version of anchoring on a data-driven pattern.
numbers: 5,383 pairs, 49 diseases, 8 departments, from 226,814 DDXPlus samples filtered to cases where the top two diagnoses differ by under 0.5% prior. Base accuracy GPT-5 54.30%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.58%, both with bias trap rate above 50%. Gemini-2.5-Pro trap rate 60.90% vs Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98%.
limits: Synthetic narratives from a simulator; LLM-judge committee (96.1% quality pass) plus four physicians; not a direct test of Patel-Groen.
agent_relevance: Pattern-first reasoning in LLMs fails when one key finding flips the diagnosis; scale does not fix it.

source: MedEinst (2026) error taxonomy for GPT-5
finding: GPT-5 failures in trap cases: over a third ignore the key discriminating symptom; the rest mostly under-analyse or over-rationalise.
numbers: Of GPT-5 error cases: 35% perceptual blindness (key evidence ignored); among those that noticed it, 43% underthinking and 22% overthinking (motivated reasoning).
limits: Classification by the authors' pipeline. The 43% and 22% are shares of the cases where the key symptom was acknowledged.
agent_relevance: Names two failure poles: too little backward checking and too much one-sided confirmation.

source: MedEinst (2026) ECR-Agent: forward causal and backward counterfactual stages
finding: Agent makes an intuitive differential, then a forward step (seek discriminating evidence), a backward step (if disease d were true, what evidence should be seen; missing evidence gets a penalty shadow node), then an audit.
numbers: Qwen3-32B: base acc / robust acc / trap rate = 40.25 / 11.86 / 43.46. Add dynamic causal inference: 55.49 / 19.94 / 38.32. Add critic graph and memory: 69.49 / 24.21 / 33.75. Debate agents MDAgent and DyLAN had robust accuracy about 8-10%.
quote: If disease d were true, what evidence should we observe?
limits: Components (graph, retrieval, memory) are bundled; the backward step's own gain is not isolated. Authors' own method and benchmark.
agent_relevance: Direct template: for each live hypothesis, list expected-but-missing findings and penalise.

source: MedEinst (2026) shadow-node scoring rule inside the agent loop
finding: Candidate score S(d) = w_m*matches - w_c*conflicts - w_s*shadow, where shadow means expected evidence that could not be verified. The shadow term is the backward-reasoning part.
numbers: Weights are hyperparameters. Shadow-node ablation alone not reported in the text read. Full agent 69.49% base accuracy on MedEinst.
limits: Needs external knowledge graph and retrieval (PubMed, OpenTargets).
agent_relevance: Approximate in context: list expected findings per hypothesis, mark each present, absent or unknown.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: One CoT prompt and four clinical-reasoning prompts (differential diagnosis, intuitive, analytic, Bayesian) on MedQA. Imitating clinician reasoning styles did not raise accuracy for GPT-4; for GPT-3.5 the differential and Bayesian styles hurt.
numbers: GPT-3.5 MedQA: CoT 46%, intuitive 48% (P=0.9), analytic 40% (-6, P=0.001), differential 38% (-8, P<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4, P=0.02). GPT-4: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78% (+2.2, P=0.24), analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4, P=0.07).
limits: Few-shot with two worked examples per prompt; MedQA is multiple choice, where forward pattern matching works; direction not tested as such.
agent_relevance: Differential-first prompting gives no reliable accuracy gain on multiple choice; the value is in visible reasoning.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: backward chaining for automated reasoning in natural language
finding: Backward (goal to facts) proof search with an LLM beats forward-chaining Selection-Inference and chain-of-thought, especially at depth 5. Forward success rate falls on later inference steps as the search space grows.
numbers: Relative gains at depth 5: ProofWriter-PUD +44% vs CoT and +56% vs SI; PrOntoQA +37% vs CoT and +113% vs SI; ParaRules +43% vs CoT.
quote: reasoning in the backward direction ... is significantly more efficient at proof-finding
limits: Synthetic logic with a defined goal; diagnosis has no single target. It points the opposite way to the Patel-Groen claim that forward is the efficient mode.
agent_relevance: In closed rule worlds, goal-driven search scales better; forward is fine when chains are short.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) FOBAR: forward-backward reasoning in LLMs for mathematical verification
finding: Combine forward self-consistency with backward verification: mask a number in the question and ask the model to recover it given a candidate answer. Gains over forward-only Self-Consistency on six math sets.
numbers: text-davinci-003 CoT: Self-Consistency 81.4 average, FOBAR 83.5. ComplexCoT: Self-Consistency 83.2, FOBAR 85.0. Self-Verification 75.8 and 78.3 in the same tables.
limits: Math with a numeric answer and a template backward question. Medicine has no such masking.
agent_relevance: Forward-only sampling saturates; a backward check adds an independent signal.

source: Weng et al. (2023) LLMs are better reasoners with self-verification
finding: Model takes its own forward answer as a condition and tries to recover the original facts (backward verification), then ranks candidates by consistency. Gains are small on average.
numbers: Average gain 2.33% on Instruct-GPT; arithmetic tasks +1.67% / +2.84%, other reasoning +0.62% / +0.78% (two settings). New SOTA on 6 of 8 datasets.
limits: Modest, task-dependent gains; FOBAR's table shows Self-Verification below Self-Consistency in several cells.
agent_relevance: Expect low single-digit gains from backward verification.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Train a student on forward reasoning, a backward question and backward reasoning from a teacher. Average 13.53% gain over student zero-shot across 12 datasets (commonsense, math, logic).
numbers: Average +13.53% over zero-shot student; forward-only symbolic distillation +6.69%. With 10% of the correct forward data it beat standard fine-tuning on 10x more forward data.
limits: Training, not scaffolding; our agent cannot fine-tune. Datasets not medical.
agent_relevance: At inference time this maps to forward-backward consistency checks.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of an LLM on the reasoning tasks of a physician (o1-preview)
finding: o1-preview, a model that reasons at length, beat GPT-4 and physicians on differential diagnosis and documented reasoning; no explicit forward or backward manipulation.
numbers: NEJM cases: correct dx in differential 78.3% (95% CI 70.7-84.8); first dx correct 52%. Exact or very close dx 88.6% vs GPT-4 72.9% on 70 shared cases. Reasoning score median 86% vs GPT-4 42%, physicians with GPT-4 41%, physicians 34%. ER triage exact or close 65.8% vs 54.4% and 48.1% for two physicians.
limits: Does not test reasoning direction. Probabilistic reasoning: o1-preview similar to GPT-4. Text-only cases.
agent_relevance: Test-time reasoning, not a prescribed direction, lifts clinical text tasks.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with LLMs
finding: A fine-tuned PaLM-2 DDx model beat unaided clinicians and helped clinicians on 302 NEJM cases. No forward or backward arm.
numbers: 302 cases: LLM top-10 accuracy 59.1% vs unassisted clinicians 33.6% (p=0.04); top-1 29.2%. Clinicians assisted by LLM 51.7% vs 36.1% unaided and 44.4% with search.
limits: Case reports differ from live practice; reasoning route not studied.
agent_relevance: Background: data-in, diagnosis-out models are strong; the debate is about route, not outcome.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) historical note on earlier DDx systems (secondary)
finding: States that NEJM cases have been the test for every differential generator from primitive Bayesian systems to rule-based systems and symptom checkers. MYCIN and INTERNIST-1 were not opened this session.
numbers: No figures.
quote: tested by every differential diagnosis generator from primitive Bayesian systems, symbolic rules-based systems
limits: Pointer only; forward/backward-chaining claims for classic systems are unverified here.
agent_relevance: Old expert systems fixed direction in code; LLM agents can choose per case.

source: Patel and Groen (1986) Knowledge-based solution strategies in medical reasoning (not opened)
finding: Founding result named in the task: experts on familiar cases reason forward from data, novices and experts on hard cases more backward. Not read this session.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Human-side numbers belong in Angle A and B files.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Coderre et al. (2003) Diagnostic reasoning strategies and diagnostic success (not opened)
finding: Recalled, not read: linked pattern recognition to diagnostic accuracy. Pointer for human-side angles. Verify before citing.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified.
agent_relevance: Background.

source: Gap note: no LLM study found that tests Patel-Groen forward vs backward directly
finding: In the papers read, forward and backward are engineering labels (symptom to diagnosis vs diagnosis to expected symptoms), not tests of expert vs novice reasoning in models. Search coverage is partial.
numbers: 0 direct tests among 10 opened sources. 3 clinical LLM papers (Dual-Inf, MSDiagnosis, MedEinst) use both directions in an agent loop; 4 non-clinical papers (LAMBADA, FOBAR, Self-Verification, RevThink) test direction on logic and math.
limits: arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors; only 2 WebSearch calls were used.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on an expert-forward claim to design the agent; use backward verification as a check.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: size of the backward-check gain
finding: Backward steps give small to moderate gains, larger in closed logic than in clinical text.
numbers: Clinical: Dual-Inf +6.1 points accuracy vs SC-CoT (GPT-4); MSDiagnosis +2.28 final F1. Math: FOBAR +2.1 and +1.8 points over Self-Consistency; Self-Verification +2.33 average. Logic: LAMBADA +37% to +113% relative at depth 5. Training: RevThink +13.53%.
limits: Different metrics, baselines and tasks; cannot be pooled. Authors' own methods; no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Budget a few points, more when the target has a checkable goal.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: naming a style versus forcing a check
finding: Asking the model to adopt a clinician reasoning style (Savage) did not raise accuracy, while adding a structured check step (Dual-Inf, ECR-Agent) did on their own benchmarks.
numbers: Savage GPT-4: differential +2.2 points (P=0.24), Bayesian -3.4 points (P=0.07). ECR-Agent trap rate 43.46 to 33.75 on Qwen3-32B. Dual-Inf +6.1 points over SC-CoT.
limits: Different tasks, so a pattern and not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Prefer operators that make the model check expected findings and missing evidence over ones that name a style.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: scale and reasoning models do not remove anchoring
finding: MedEinst finds the highest base-accuracy models the most trap-prone, and reasoning-optimised models (DeepSeek-R1) still fail; Brodeur finds long-reasoning o1 strong on ordinary NEJM cases.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.58% base accuracy with 60.90% trap rate; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98% trap rate; o1-preview 78.3% correct in differential on NEJM cases.
limits: MedEinst is adversarial by construction (prior gap under 0.5%); NEJM cases are not. Single studies.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit disconfirmation step when the first hypothesis fits the common pattern.
